3. Data Cleaning

This code checks for missing values, duplicates, incorrect data types, and invalid values. It also documents the cleaning process with comments, as your instructor requires.

Python

# Check for missing values
print("Missing values:")
print(df.isnull().sum())

# Check for duplicates
print("Duplicate rows:", df.duplicated().sum())
print("Duplicate IDs:", df["id"].duplicated().sum())

# Remove duplicate records
df = df.drop_duplicates()
df = df.drop_duplicates(subset="id")

# Replace blank text with missing values
df = df.replace(r"^\s*$", np.nan, regex=True)

# Convert the timestamp to a readable date
df["time"] = pd.to_datetime(
df["time"], unit="ms", utc=True, errors="coerce"
)

# Convert numeric columns to numeric data types
for col in ["mag", "depth", "latitude", "longitude"]:
df[col] = pd.to_numeric(df[col], errors="coerce")

# Remove non-earthquake events
df = df[df["type"] == "earthquake"].copy()

# Remove rows missing important information
df = df.dropna(subset=[
"id", "time", "mag", "depth",
"latitude", "longitude"
])

Step 4: Data Manipulation — Global Earthquakes

For this part of your final project, we'll use Sorting, Filtering, and Grouping with Pandas. This meets your instructor's requirement of at least two operations.

Copy and paste the following code into a new cell in Google Colab, after you've uploaded your cleaned CSV.

Python Code

Python

import pandas as pd

# 1. SORTING
# Sort earthquakes by magnitude, highest to lowest
largest_earthquakes = df.sort_values(
by="mag", ascending=False
)

print("Top 10 Largest Earthquakes:")
display(largest_earthquakes[
["place", "mag", "depth"]
].head(10))


# 2. FILTERING
# Find earthquakes with a magnitude of 6.0 or higher
strong_earthquakes = df[df["mag"] >= 6.0]

print("Earthquakes with Magnitude 6.0 or Higher:")
print("Total:", len(strong_earthquakes))
display(strong_earthquakes[
["place", "mag", "depth"]
].head(10))


# 3. GROUPING
# Calculate earthquake counts and average magnitudes
# for each tectonic region
region_summary = df.groupby(
"tectonic_region"
).agg(
earthquake_count=("mag", "count"),
average_magnitude=("mag", "mean"),
average_depth=("depth", "mean")
).round(2)

What each operation does

Operation

Purpose

Sorting

Identifies the largest earthquakes in the dataset.

Filtering

Focuses on stronger earthquakes with magnitudes of 6.0 or higher.

Grouping

Compares earthquake frequency, average magnitude, and depth across tectonic regions.

Step 5: Data Visualization — Global Earthquakes

For your final project, we'll create four visualizations using Matplotlib and Seaborn. This exceeds your instructor's requirement of three.

Each chart will have a title, axis labels, and formatting. The code will also save each chart as a PNG image for your GitHub README.

1. Import the libraries and create a folder

Run this code first in Google Colab. It uses the df DataFrame you already loaded.

Python

import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import seaborn as sns
import os

# Create a folder to save project charts
os.makedirs("visualizations", exist_ok=True)

# Set chart style
sns.set_theme(style="whitegrid")

2. Bar Chart — Earthquakes by Tectonic Region

This chart shows which tectonic regions experienced the most earthquakes in your dataset.

Python

plt.figure(figsize=(11, 6))

# Count earthquakes by tectonic region
region_counts = df["tectonic_region"].value_counts()

sns.barplot(
x=region_counts.values,
y=region_counts.index,
color="steelblue"
)

plt.title("Number of Earthquakes by Tectonic Region")
plt.xlabel("Number of Earthquakes")
plt.ylabel("Tectonic Region")
plt.tight_layout()

# Save chart
plt.savefig("visualizations/earthquakes_by_region.png", dpi=300)
plt.show()

Example of the chart using your previously reported data

  • Pacific Ring of Fire: Earthquakes 8.4K
  • Alpide-Himalayan: Earthquakes 669
  • Mid-ocean ridges: Earthquakes 606
  • Intraplate: Earthquakes 336

Counts from earlier dataset analysis

Insight: The Pacific Ring of Fire has the highest number of recorded earthquakes in this dataset.

3. Histogram — Earthquake Magnitude Distribution

This chart shows how frequently different earthquake magnitudes occur.

Python

plt.figure(figsize=(10, 6))

sns.histplot(
data=df,
x="mag",
bins=25,
color="orange",
edgecolor="black"
)

plt.title("Distribution of Earthquake Magnitudes")
plt.xlabel("Earthquake Magnitude")
plt.ylabel("Number of Earthquakes")
plt.tight_layout()

# Save chart
plt.savefig("visualizations/magnitude_distribution.png", dpi=300)
plt.show()

Insight to investigate: Are smaller-magnitude earthquakes more common than larger ones?

4. Scatter Plot — Magnitude vs. Depth

This chart compares earthquake magnitude with depth to see whether the two variables are related.

Python

plt.figure(figsize=(10, 6))

sns.scatterplot(
data=df,
x="depth",
y="mag",
alpha=0.4,
color="purple",
label="Earthquakes"
)

plt.title("Earthquake Magnitude vs. Depth")
plt.xlabel("Depth (km)")
plt.ylabel("Magnitude")
plt.legend()
plt.tight_layout()

# Save chart
plt.savefig("visualizations/magnitude_vs_depth.png", dpi=300)
plt.show()

# Calculate correlation
correlation = df["mag"].corr(df["depth"])
print("Magnitude vs. Depth Correlation:", round(correlation, 3))

Insight: Your earlier dataset analysis showed a correlation of approximately −0.046, suggesting almost no linear relationship between earthquake magnitude and depth.

5. Line Chart — Earthquakes Over Time

This chart shows how the number of recorded earthquakes changes each month.

Python

# Convert time to datetime if necessary
if pd.api.types.is_numeric_dtype(df["time"]):
df["time"] = pd.to_datetime(
df["time"], unit="ms", utc=True
)
else:
df["time"] = pd.to_datetime(
df["time"], utc=True
)

# Count earthquakes by month
monthly_counts = (
df.set_index("time")
.resample("MS")
.size()
)

plt.figure(figsize=(12, 6))

plt.plot(
monthly_counts.index,
monthly_counts.values,
marker="o",
color="green",
label="Monthly Earthquakes"
)

plt.title("Earthquake Frequency Over Time")
plt.xlabel("Month")
plt.ylabel("Number of Earthquakes")
plt.xticks(rotation=45)
plt.legend()
plt.tight_layout()

# Save chart

Insight to investigate: This visualization can reveal months with higher or lower earthquake activity in the dataset. Partial months at the beginning and end of the date range should be interpreted carefully.
